cases.name: Base case
cases.assumption: Aftermarket sales grow 8% a year and margins hold near 53%. Cash builds on the balance sheet.
cases.leavesOut: acquisitions and any further special dividend.

cases.name: Downside case
cases.assumption: Flight hours fall 10% in FY26 and recover half in FY27; prices stay flat; floating debt costs 100 basis points more.

bottomLine.lead: Leverage falls only if the cash is kept: net debt drops from 5.9x to 3.8x EBITDA by FY27 in the base case, and cash flow covers interest about three times throughout.
bottomLine.rest: The downside case holds leverage above 5x and still funds interest from operations. Debt is not repaid in either case, and about USD 17 billion falls due between 2028 and 2030.

findings.title: Deleveraging depends on keeping the cash
findings.text: Gross debt stays at USD 29.7 billion in both cases. Net leverage falls from 5.9x to 3.8x by FY27 only because free cash flow is left on the balance sheet.

findings.title: Earnings quality is high
findings.text: Margins have risen every year since FY22, and aftermarket sales, the most profitable part of the business, are over half of revenue.

findings.title: Interest is covered with room to spare
findings.text: Cover stays between 2.3x and 3.6x across both cases. The low point is FY26 in the downside case.

findings.title: Refinancing is concentrated in 2028 to 2030
findings.text: About USD 17 billion, 57% of debt, falls due in those three years. The model assumes it is refinanced at current spreads.

contrary.title: The cash may not stay
contrary.text: The company has paid out its cash build three times in five years. If it does so again, leverage stays near 6x and the base case deleveraging does not happen.

watch.title: Two levels to watch
watch.text: Net leverage above 7.0x for two quarters, or interest cover below 2.0x, would turn this view negative. A public commitment to hold leverage below 5x would improve it.
